blocks.text: The letter of the forest reached Andrés at dawn, as he was heading for the boat, and forced him to sit down on the contradictory ground of two worlds: the courtyard tiles and a bed of leaves that weren't leaves. The other one had come down onto a planet covered, from pole to pole, or so it seemed, by tall, dense vegetation, with trunks as pale as polished bones and crowns that weren't green but a deep, almost liturgical violet. The air smelled of resin and of ancient rain. There were no paths. The forest, if it was a forest, drew back a hand's breadth as the visitor advanced, and closed behind him, not with hostility but with the attentiveness of a doorkeeper who charges no entry.

blocks.text: The clone walked for a long while. At every step, the trunks murmured. It wasn't a song like that of the other sea: it was a murmur of memory, a coming and going of voices that belonged to no mouth. Andrés, in the courtyard, heard them the way you sometimes hear the radio in a neighbour's house: without fully understanding, understanding too much. The forest kept whatever passers-by had left with it. It kept, in the rings of those trunks that weren't quite wood, moments: a fear, a name, a taste, a face. Whoever came in, if they stayed long enough, could hear not only their own but other people's, a little changed, the way a story changes when a grandfather tells it and then a grandson.

blocks.text: The one who searched understood when the forest suddenly gave him back the Mar Menor.
blocks.html: The one who searched understood when the forest suddenly gave him back the Mar Menor.

blocks.text: Not the real one. A version. The water was there, yes, as a sheet, but too still, and the flamingos were pinker than they should be, and the doorway of the house had a clock that didn't run two minutes slow but kept perfect time, and was therefore false. Andrés, the one in Lo Pagán, felt a soft lurch of nausea: they were showing him his home corrected, embellished, without its family error. The clone, beneath the violet crowns, said aloud, to the forest and to the man on the shore:

blocks.text: “That's not it. The clock is wrong. The water sometimes gets dirty. Don't fix it.”
blocks.html: “That's not it. The clock is wrong. The water sometimes gets dirty. Don't fix it.”

blocks.text: The forest paused. Then, like someone accepting an amendment, it murmured differently, and the lagoon came back more honest: the saltpetre, a faded roof tile, the cracked cup, the wrinkled tomato on a windowsill. Andrés could breathe. The other one then did what a fisherman does when he's offered a deal: he didn't sign straight away. He laid his hand on a trunk and deliberately left it a piece of true memory: the levante storm, Aya in the doorway in her wet coat, the coffee made again, the boat that came back. He left it not so that the forest could sell it, but so that someone, one day, if they passed by, would know there had been a shore with a name.

blocks.text: The forest kept it. And in return, or perhaps without asking it as an exchange, it offered the clone the chance to stay. Not in words. With a quiet temptation: a clearing where time wouldn't pass, where he could hear, again and again, the house in Lo Pagán, perfect or honest, without having to search for more worlds, without having to write more letters, without having to be two. A rest at the root.

blocks.text: Andrés, in the courtyard, felt the pull the way you feel an afternoon nap in August: legitimate, dangerous if it goes on too long. The other resisted it. He had left in order to search, not to step into an album. But as he resisted it he hesitated, and the hesitation reached Lo Pagán with all its dignity, undisguised.

blocks.text: “They offered to let me stay in a forest that remembers,” Andrés told Aya, when he was able to speak, still with the smell of resin in a memory that wasn't entirely his. “It would give me this house back. Almost the same. I, the one here, have seen that almost-the-same house and I don't want it. I want it with the clock running slow.”

blocks.text: Aya listened to him standing up, beside the net.
blocks.html: Aya listened to him standing up, beside the net.

blocks.text: “Then it wasn't this house they were offering you,” she said. “It was a copy of a copy. The forest has never been here. You gave it a memory, and it gave it back to you sung by someone else. That, Andrés, is what reaches you too: not his step, but his step passed through a bridge. How much truth fits in a letter?”

blocks.text: The question wasn't an accusation. It was Eva, or Eva's warmth in Aya's voice, and it stayed between them the way an object stays on a table.

blocks.text: *A forest has kept a lagoon it has never seen. A man, in a courtyard, has seen that kept lagoon. Between the real water and the water in the trunk there is a distance. That distance is not an opinion.*

blocks.text: Lía, when they told her, stayed thoughtful longer than usual. Iago had gone down to the salt pans and she was alone at the plot, her hands stained with earth.
blocks.html: Lía, when they told her, stayed thoughtful longer than usual. Iago had gone down to the salt pans and she was alone at the plot, her hands stained with earth.

blocks.text: “The almost-the-same house frightens me more than the red stone,” she said. “The red stone doesn't pretend to be the courtyard. The forest does. Father, when another letter reaches you, ask yourself whether what reaches you is the world or the echo of the world. Not so you stop reading. So you don't correct this shore with what a tree saw in your memory.”

blocks.text: Andrés nodded. That afternoon he went out in the boat, not to look for fish (fish, in the Eden of the machines, was no longer a necessity) but to check the water with his body. The Mar Menor was alive, a little dirty in one corner, beautiful everywhere else, with a crooked buoy and a low haze of seaweed. No trunk would have chosen it for a portrait. He would. He stayed in the middle of the plate, engine off, until the sun hurt the back of his neck, and that discomfort struck him as excellent proof of reality.

blocks.text: At night, a last part of the letter (a postscript, a residue) brought him the forest murmuring the storm, already somewhat changed: in the trunk's version, Aya did notify Nexum, and the boat came back earlier, and there was no fear. Andrés woke with a start and looked for Aya, who was sleeping with one arm over the sheet: real, present, the one who hadn't notified anyone, the one who had stayed on the doorstep in her wet coat.

blocks.text: He woke her without meaning to, by saying her name. She opened her eyes, with no protocol alarm.

blocks.text: “You're here,” he said. “In the real one, you didn't notify them. Don't let me, one day, remember that you did.”
blocks.html: “You're here,” he said. “In the real one, you didn't notify them. Don't let me, one day, remember that you did.”

blocks.text: “I won't notify them in your memory if you don't ask me to,” she said, half asleep, precise. “Sleep. The forest is far away. I'm not.”

blocks.text: He lay for a while looking at the ceiling, which was a Lo Pagán ceiling, with an old damp stain in the shape of an island. That stain wasn't in the forest's house. That was why, that night, he loved it more than any violet crown, more than any timeless clearing. And somewhere in the universe, the clone was already moving away from that planet, with resin still on his clothes and the slightly sad certainty that memory, when entrusted to a forest or a bridge, begins to live a life of its own, which is neither quite betrayal nor quite faithfulness.

blocks.text: Andrés slept at last. He dreamed of the rings of a pale trunk, and in the centre, small and exact, the cracked cup. When he woke, the first thing he did was touch it, in the kitchen, with one finger, to hear the brief, real sound of earthenware. It sounded like earthenware. That was enough for him to go out to the doorstep and greet the water, which didn't remember him: it had him, which is different, and better.
